selinger1979.title: Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System
selinger1979.author: P. Griffiths Selinger, M. M. Astrahan, D. D. Chamberlin, R. A. Lorie, T. G. Price
selinger1979.venue: ACM SIGMOD 1979, pp. 23-34 — Proceedings of the 1979 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, ISBN 0-89791-001-X. The scan's own copyright line on p.23 reads "01979 ACM0-89791-001-X/79/0500-0023 $00.75" (OCR of ©1979 ACM 0-89791-001-X/79/0500-0023 $00.75), so the proceedings ISBN and the May-1979 date code are in the paper's front matter; the printed folios run 23 to 34. Byline reads "IBM Research Division, San Jose, California 95193"; body says the system "was designed and built by members of the IBM San Jose Research Laboratory".
selinger1979.quote: More precisely, we say that a predicate or set of predicates matches an index access path when the predicates are sargable and the columns mentioned in the predicate(s) are an initial substring of the set of columns of the index key.
quotes: More precisely, we say that a predicate or set of predicates matches an index access path when the predicates are sargable and the columns mentioned in the predicate(s) are an initial substring of the set of columns of the index key.
For example, a NAME, LOCATION index matches NAME = 'SMITH' AND LOCATION = 'SAN JOSE'.
These formulas give index pages fetched plus data pages fetched plus the weighting factor times RSI tuple retrieval calls.
This assumes an even distribution of tuples among the index key values.
Note that this assumes that column values are independent.
We assume that a lack of statistics implies that the relation is small, so an arbitrary factor is chosen.
Preliminary results indicate that, although the costs predicted by the optimizer are often not accurate in absolute value, the true optimal path is selected in a large majority of cases.
For a two-way join, the cost of optimization is approximately equivalent to between 5 and 20 database retrievals.
selinger1979.note: Read as a scanned PDF, text extracted with pdftotext. The scan's OCR substitutes the letter l for the digit 1 (Table 1 prints as "F = l/10 otherwise") and breaks lines across the two-column layout; digits restored, line breaks joined, and stray OCR punctuation dropped from inside words ("costs p.redicted", "retrie,vals", "For example."); wording is verbatim. Table 1 gives F = 1 / ICARD(column index) when an index exists on the column and F = 1/10 otherwise.
supports: leftmost-prefix rule defined in 1979 as an 'initial substring' of the index key columns
cost measured in index pages fetched plus data pages fetched plus weighted CPU (RSI) calls
1/10 default selectivity for an equality predicate on an unindexed column
the authors' own admission that predicted costs are often not accurate in absolute value

selinger2003.title: Pat Selinger Speaks Out on Why System R Was So Successful, Interactions with the INGRES and QBE Teams, How to Do Techology Transfer, How to Manage Difficult People, How to Mentor 3,000 People at Once, and More
selinger2003.author: Marianne Winslett (interviewer); Patricia Selinger (subject)
selinger2003.venue: ACM SIGMOD Record, Vol. 32, No. 4, December 2003, pp. 93-103. Interview recorded in San Diego at the 2003 SIGMOD/PODS conference.
selinger2003.quote: Boeing was one of the early users and they said, “[System R] is a tremendous tool, but our problem is that it is [only] February and we have [already] used up our computing [time] budget for the year[, from running so many database queries]!”
quotes: Boeing was one of the early users and they said, “[System R] is a tremendous tool, but our problem is that it is [only] February and we have [already] used up our computing [time] budget for the year[, from running so many database queries]!”

And I said, “Oh, we’re so sorry, we’re really sorry!” And they said, “No, [don’t apologise, System R] is wonderful. We can ask questions we could never find the answers to before. We’re now able to do more than we could ever do before.”

I came with a background in operating systems and programming languages, but I knew nothing about databases. So they gave me Chris Date’s book and said, “Here, read this, and then start interacting with the rest of us after you’re finished.”
I came to IBM when the System R platform was just getting launched.
her 1979 SIGMOD paper, “Access Path Selection in a Relation Database Management System,” set forth the guiding principles that underlie the query optimizers in every major database system today
At that time there were maybe 30-40 people who came in and out of the project
selinger2003.note: Square brackets are the published interview's own editorial insertions and are reproduced here. The intro line misprints the paper's title as "Relation" where the paper itself reads "Relational". Everything Selinger says about Boeing and about her own arrival is a 2003 recollection of the 1970s and is undated in the source; the prose says "told an interviewer in 2003" for exactly this reason.
supports: Boeing exhausted its annual computing budget by February and called System R a tremendous tool anyway
Selinger arrived at System R from operating systems and programming languages knowing nothing about databases
the 1979 paper's principles underlie the query optimizers in every major database system

unverified: The calendar year of the Boeing budget remark. Selinger recalls it in 2003 without a date; System R's customer trials are not dated in either source I opened, so no year is given in the prose.

The exact wording of the paper's cost formula line 'COST = PAGE FETCHES + W * (RSI CALLS)'. The scan OCRs it as 'COST = PAGE -FETCHES + W * (RSI CALLS).' with a stray hyphen, so the prose quotes the Table 2 sentence instead, which extracted cleanly.

The SIGMOD 1979 conference city and dates. dl.acm.org returns HTTP 403, and the scan carries no conference header. The venue, the 23-34 page range and the DOI 10.1145/582095.582099 are corroborated by dblp's proceedings record, which agrees with the ISBN and the 0500 (May 1979) date code printed in the paper's own copyright line; the city and dates rest on dblp alone and appear nowhere in the prose or on a card.

That Oracle's engineers read the published System R papers and shipped a commercial SQL database before IBM did. Widely repeated, no source opened for it, so it appears nowhere in the prose or on a card.

Whether the 'stop at the first range predicate' refinement of matching-column counting is in the 1979 paper. The paper's matching definition covers sargable predicates and an initial substring of the key columns and says nothing about ranges terminating the count; that refinement is DB2 documentation, so it is not attributed to Selinger anywhere here.
